title: Wire Jev into Grok Bot: a shadow-first router skill
description: Add a Jev router skill to Grok Bot: keep the API key out of chat, log a shadow week, gate skips in code, keep approvals human and a kill switch ready.

source.title: How To Wire Jev Into Grok Bot: The Best Agent I've Built

guide_authors.name: Appit Studio
guide_authors.role: Original editorial guide; AI-assisted research, drafting and offline verification

image.alt: Three stages of a Grok Bot router rollout: code checks side effects first, Jev picks one of four skip actions in shadow mode, and code-owned confidence floors decide what active mode may skip

connections.step: Start from an inspectable router module, skill file, config and kill switch instead of generating them from scratch
connections.why: The pinned reference package implements the same shape the article describes: a jev-usage-router skill, shadow and active modes, an enabled flag and a bypass marker, plus code-side checks that a cached artifact exists before reuse. rody does not name or endorse it.
connections.limitations: MIT reference package with no tagged release; Python with typesafe-sdk and PyYAML. Defaults to the moving jev-latest alias and illustrative thresholds. Shadow mode still calls TypeSafe when enabled; active mode works only if the skill is honoured. Its A/B notes are one local proxy run. Only the disabled dry run was executed for this guide; no live inference.

connections.step: Use a stricter preflight envelope when the main risk is consequential tool use rather than wasted retries
connections.why: grok-jev-guard puts local hard stops for secrets, deletion and payments ahead of Jev judgments and returns proceed, scope_down, checkpoint, ask_human or block. That is closer to an approval layer than to the article's cost router.
connections.limitations: MIT Python 0.1.0 package; Python 3.11+ and a TypeSafe key for live judgments. Catalog review inspected source only; not run for this guide. Its envelope is advisory unless the bot's skill enforces it.

faqs.question: Does Jev replace the model that runs Grok Bot?
faqs.answer: No. Grok Bot still plans, writes and uses tools. The router asks Jev one bounded question before expensive steps, such as whether to reuse an artifact or stop a failing retry, and the skill decides what to do with the answer.

faqs.question: Is the TypeSafe key safe on the Grok Bot computer?
faqs.answer: It is kept out of chat and files, but every bot on the account shares the same computer and can read the environment variable. Use a dedicated key with a spending limit, rotate it if a bot handles untrusted content, and never log it.

faqs.question: Why run the router in shadow mode first?
faqs.answer: Shadow mode records what the router would have done while the agent keeps working normally. Comparing those records with what actually happened shows whether stop_retry or research_capped would have cut off work that later succeeded, before the router is allowed to act.

faqs.question: Should Jev decide when to ask a human?
faqs.answer: Not for side effects. Sending, publishing, paying and deleting are known from the tool being called, so code should require approval for them before any Jev call. Jev can still suggest asking for help when a task is ambiguous.

faqs.question: What happens if the Jev call fails?
faqs.answer: The router should return proceed and record the error, so the agent does the work it would have done anyway. A provider failure must not silently skip work, and it must never remove an approval step.

faqs.question: Does shadow mode avoid TypeSafe charges?
faqs.answer: No. Shadow mode still sends each router state to TypeSafe and may be billed; it only ignores the answer. To stop calls entirely, set enabled to false.
